newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish right-wing feud hinders secularist pact.
newsitem.headline: Turkish right-wing feud hinders secularist pact.

text.p: Turkey's rival conservatives squabbled their way through talks about a planned secularist alliance on Tuesday, in a bitter feud that gives hope to the flagging Islamists.
Faction leader Tansu Ciller said she had refused to even consider an offer from prime minister-designate Mesut Yilmaz to forge an anti-Islamist government under his leadership.
"I did not discuss the government issue, so as not to legitimise Yilmaz's position," Ciller told reporters after a 20-minute meeting between the pair.
Ciller, the caretaker deputy prime minister, says President Suleyman Demirel should have named her instead of Yilmaz to replace the pro-Islamic coalition that collapsed last week.
She heads a partnership with the Islam-based Welfare Party that is stronger in parliament than Yilmaz's group.
Fading investor confidence in the government search brought Istanbul shares back down to earth following a leap of eight percent on Monday. The main index closed down 5.07 points.
"The market was irritated by the possibility that (Ciller's) conservative True Path Party may not support the new alliance," said Okan Gulek from Taksim Securities.

A key leftist and a conservative splinter leader said they would back Yilmaz, but the anti-Islamists are still around a dozen votes short of the simple majority needed to win a confidence vote in the 550-member parliament.
Ciller, a U.S.-educated technocrat, accuses Yilmaz of trying to poach her MPs. Aides said Tuesday's meeting was stormy.

"You will never, ever win the confidence vote," a party source who witnessed the talks quoted Ciller as telling her rival. "Give the mandate back (to the president) immediately. You are doing democracy a disservice," she said.
"It is actually you and your behaviour that are damaging democracy," replied Yilmaz, the main opposition figure.
The pair are pro-market political soul mates born within a few months of each other but the fight for control of the right has highlighted a clash of their personalities.
She is an astute political operator who thinks on her feet while he is staid and pensive. Their animosity caused the downfall of a three-month-old conservative coalition last year.

Ciller, 51, then went into government with Welfare despite vowing never to do so. The Islamists had taken advantage of the split in the right-wing vote to narrowly win general elections in 1995 and were pressing corruption charges against her.

Ciller became Turkey's first woman prime minister in 1993. She said on Tuesday she would offer her opponent the chance to join a coalition led by her if he failed to drum up enough support in the coming days.
"When we get the mandate we will ask Yilmaz to come and join us in a broad-based government," she said. Yilmaz has vowed to have a cabinet list ready by the start of next week.
The outgoing Islamist prime minister, Necmettin Erbakan, gave Yilmaz little chance of filling his shoes.

"As soon as parliament refuses a vote of confidence in a Yilmaz government, he will have to hand back the mandate. I believe this will be obvious tomorrow at the latest," Erbakan told a meeting of his Welfare deputies.
Erbakan, the first Islamist to lead modern Turkey, resigned last week after months of pressure from the staunchly secularist army to clamp down on Islamist activism.
"A new government with a genuine majority in parliament will be formed," Erbakan said in reference to plans to revamp his coalition under Ciller.
